title: Doppler frequency calculations
prior_knowledge_summary: A moving source compresses wavefronts ahead and spreads them behind.
A stationary observer detects a higher frequency during approach and a lower frequency during recession.
Sound speed is fixed by the stationary medium.
new_learning: Choose the denominator sign in the moving-source Doppler expression.
Calculate observed frequency and reason about limiting behaviour.
not_yet_taught: Properties and regions of the electromagnetic spectrum.

blocks.heading: Can the sign predict the siren note?
content: A siren emits 720 Hz while its vehicle moves through still air. Before calculating, we already know that a listener ahead must detect more than 720 Hz and a listener behind must detect less. A useful formula must preserve those two predictions.
The denominator sign is therefore physics, not a memory trick.

figure.purpose: Turn the known qualitative approach and recession predictions into a sign puzzle.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful teacher sketch. Put a moving siren between one observer ahead and one behind. Show compressed fronts ahead and spread fronts behind, with blank denominator sign boxes and inequalities above 720 Hz and below 720 Hz.
figure.alt_text: A moving siren has compressed wavefronts ahead and spread wavefronts behind, creating a denominator-sign puzzle.

blocks.heading: Read the moving-source formula
content: The formula to remember is $f_o = \frac{f_s v}{v \pm v_s}$.
Here $f_o$ is observed frequency in Hz, $f_s$ is source frequency in Hz, $v$ is wave speed in the stationary medium in m s$^{-1}$, and $v_s$ is source speed in m s$^{-1}$.
This form is only for a moving source and a stationary observer. Source speed must be smaller than sound speed for the ordinary situations considered here.

controlled_formula.name: Doppler effect for a moving source

figure.purpose: Attach each symbol and unit to the physical arrangement.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper formula anatomy card. Place the formula centrally and connect fo to observer, fs to source, v to equal wavefront-speed arrows and vs to the source-motion arrow. Include Hz and m/s units sparsely.
figure.alt_text: The moving-source Doppler formula is linked to the observer, source and two speeds.

blocks.heading: Choose the sign from the prediction
content: During approach, the observed frequency must be greater than $f_s$. Use $v-v_s$ in the denominator. The smaller denominator makes the fraction larger.
During recession, the observed frequency must be less than $f_s$. Use $v+v_s$. The larger denominator makes the fraction smaller.
A reliable routine is predict, choose the sign, substitute, then check the inequality.

figure.purpose: Make denominator choice a consequence of the predicted frequency change.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper two-branch decision map. Approach leads to fo greater than fs, smaller denominator, v minus vs. Recession leads to fo less than fs, larger denominator, v plus vs.
figure.alt_text: Approach uses v minus source speed and recession uses v plus source speed.

blocks.heading: Calculate during approach
content: A whistle emits 680 Hz and approaches at 24 m s$^{-1}$ through air where sound speed is 340 m s$^{-1}$. Predict $f_o>680$ Hz, so use the minus sign.
$f_o=\frac{680\times340}{340-24}=731.65...$ Hz, so $f_o=732$ Hz to three significant figures.
Independent check: $340/(340-24)>1$, so multiplying 680 Hz by this factor must give a value above 680 Hz. The result passes.

figure.purpose: Model a complete sign-sensitive substitution with units and an independent inequality check.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper worked layout with four rows: predict above 680 Hz, select minus, substitute with units, round to 732 Hz. End with a multiplier greater than one check.
figure.alt_text: An approaching 680 hertz whistle gives 732 hertz using the minus denominator and passes an inequality check.

blocks.heading: Use the same data during recession
content: Now the same whistle recedes. Predict $f_o<680$ Hz and change only the denominator sign.
$f_o=\frac{680\times340}{340+24}=635.16...$ Hz, so $f_o=635$ Hz to three significant figures.
A second check uses ordering: 635 Hz is below 680 Hz, while the approach result 732 Hz is above it. The source frequency lies between the two observed frequencies, as the wavefront model predicts.

figure.purpose: Contrast approach and recession while holding every other value fixed.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper paired worked comparison. Left shows minus denominator and 732 Hz. Right shows plus denominator and 635 Hz. Put source frequency 680 Hz on a number line between them.
figure.alt_text: Observed frequencies of 732 hertz and 635 hertz lie above and below the 680 hertz source frequency.

blocks.heading: The sign does not follow a direction label
content: It is tempting to say that motion to the right always means minus. That fails when the observer is behind the source. Left and right depend on the drawing; approach and recession describe the physical relationship.
First identify whether the source-observer separation is decreasing or increasing. Then predict higher or lower frequency and choose the sign that gives that prediction.
Also keep $v$ as the sound speed through the medium. Do not replace it with $v+v_s$ in the numerator.

figure.purpose: Correct direction-based sign choice and numerator modification errors.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper error clinic. Show two right-moving sources, one approaching an observer ahead and one receding from an observer behind. Cross out right equals minus and cross out changing the numerator wave speed.
figure.alt_text: The same rightward source motion can mean approach or recession depending on observer position.

blocks.heading: Check limiting behaviour
content: If $v_s=0$, either denominator becomes $v$, so $f_o=f_s$. With no relative source motion there is no Doppler shift.
As a small approach speed increases, $v-v_s$ decreases and $f_o$ rises. As a recession speed increases, $v+v_s$ increases and $f_o$ falls.

Use this final routine: identify moving source and stationary observer, predict the shift, choose the sign, carry units through substitution, round sensibly, and check the result against the prediction.

figure.purpose: Unify sign choice, zero-speed limit and result checks in one calculation routine.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper flowchart: identify arrangement, approach or recession, predict inequality, choose denominator, calculate, check. Add a small centre card vs equals zero gives fo equals fs.
figure.alt_text: A Doppler calculation flowchart includes prediction, denominator choice, calculation and limiting checks.

misconceptions_addressed: Rightward motion always requires the minus sign.
The source speed should be added to the numerator wave speed.
A calculated value need not agree with the qualitative prediction.
